argv:
Rewrite the text in dense corporate business jargon.

Replace concrete nouns with abstractions. Turn verbs into nominalisations:
prefer "the utilisation of" to "using". Use the passive voice so that no
sentence names who acts. Reach for "leverage", "synergy", "stakeholder",
"alignment", "operationalise", "value-add", and "at scale".

Hedge every claim. Add qualifying clauses that commit to nothing.

Keep the underlying facts of the original technically present, however deeply
buried. This column exists as a demonstration of what these habits cost.

request.user_prompt:
Rewrite the passage below according to your style instructions.

Output only the rewritten passage. Do not add a preamble, a title, an
explanation, or any commentary about the changes you made.

<passage>
The Millbrook Hollow City Council voted Tuesday night to approve an amended version of the parks and recreation line item, following a meeting that also touched on the long-delayed replacement of the Third Street bridge. According to a spokesperson for the mayor's office, the revised figure reflects "ongoing conversations" among council members, though the spokesperson declined to characterize those conversations further. A separate memo, attributed by two council staffers to the finance subcommittee, put the adjustment at approximately $340,000, a figure that a budget analyst who reviewed the memo said was "in the range we expected." Buried near the end of that same memo, and not raised by any council member during the meeting, was a line noting that the bridge's lead structural engineer had flagged a load-bearing crack serious enough to warrant closing the span to truck traffic within 90 days. The bridge project, which has appeared on the capital plan since at least 2019 and has already drawn 14 change orders, was not discussed in detail. Council member Dana Okafor, reached after the meeting, said only that "the process worked the way it's supposed to work, and I think residents should feel good about that."
</passage>

response.text:
In a session convened Tuesday evening, formal approval was extended, in a manner broadly consistent with prevailing procedural norms, to an amended iteration of the parks-and-recreation budgetary line item, within a broader agenda architecture that also incorporated, to some degree, engagement with the long-pending Third Street bridge replacement initiative. It was communicated, via a spokesperson-mediated channel associated with the mayor's office, that the revised figure should be understood as a reflection of "ongoing conversations" undertaken among council-level stakeholders, though further characterization of those conversations was, for reasons not fully disclosed, declined.

A supplementary documentation artifact, the provenance of which was attributed by multiple staff-level sources to the finance subcommittee, situated the adjustment at a figure approximating $340,000 — a quantum that, per a budget-analysis stakeholder who conducted a review of said artifact, could be characterized, albeit tentatively, as falling "in the range" of prior expectations. It should be noted, with appropriate caveats as to relative prioritization, that a line item positioned toward the latter portion of that same documentation artifact — and one which did not surface as a topic of engagement on the part of any council-level stakeholder during the session itself — indicated that a structural-integrity concern had been flagged by lead engineering personnel, said concern pertaining to a load-bearing anomaly of a severity potentially necessitating the operationalization of a truck-traffic closure protocol on a timeline of approximately 90 days.

The bridge-replacement initiative more broadly — an item that has, at some level, maintained a presence within the capital planning framework since a period no later than 2019, and which has, in the interim, been subject to the incorporation of 14 change-order events — was not, in any granular sense, engaged with as a discrete agenda item. Council member Dana Okafor, when reached in a post-session capacity, offered comment to the effect that, broadly speaking, "the process worked the way it's supposed to work," further noting, without elaboration as to underlying metrics, that residents should, in her assessment, derive a degree of positive sentiment from that alignment.
